items.stem: What is light ?
items.answer: Light is the form of energy which gives sensation of vision.

items.stem: What kind of wave is light ?
items.answer: Light is an electromagnetic wave.

items.stem: What is image ?
items.answer: Image of an object is formed when reflected or refracted rays intersect each other.

items.stem: What is real image ?
items.answer: Real image is formed by real intersection of refracted or reflected rays.

items.stem: What is virtual image ?
items.answer: Virtual image is formed by the virtual intersection of refracted or reflected rays.

items.stem: For regular reflection what is relation between angle of incidence and angle of reflection ?
items.answer: Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection.

items.stem: When a ray is made incident normal to the plane, what is angle of incidence and angle of reflection ?
items.answer: The angle of incidence and angle of reflection both are of zero degree (0°).

items.stem: Write the mirror formula.
items.answer: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, where v is the image distance, u the object distance and f the focal length of the mirror.

items.stem: Write one use of concave and convex mirrors each.
items.answer: Concave mirror is used in solar concentration, while convex mirror is used as rear view mirror in automobiles.

items.stem: Why do we use convex mirror for side-view mirror ?
items.answer: Convex mirror is used for side view because it forms a virtual, erect and smaller (diminished) image, which gives a large field of view.

items.stem: Define the focus of a spherical mirror.
items.answer: The virtual or real point on the principal axis where all the light rays parallel to the principal axis meet after reflection is called the principal focus.

items.stem: What is centre of curvature of convex mirror ?
items.answer: The convex mirror is a part of a hollow sphere having its inward surface polished. The inside centre of that sphere is called the centre of curvature of the convex mirror.

items.stem: State laws of refraction of light.

Total power of the combination,

Since P = 1/f (f in metre),
f = 1/P = 1/(−1) = −1 m = −100 cm
The focal length of the combination is −1 m.

items.answer: (i) The power of a lens is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length in metres: P = 1/f (in metres). (ii) A positive sign indicates a convex (converging) lens; a negative sign indicates a concave (diverging) lens. (iii) The S.I. unit of power is the dioptre (D), where 1 dioptre = 1/focal length (in m). Thus 1 D is the power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre.

items.stem: The absolute refractive indices of glass and water are 4/3 and 3/2 respectively. If the speed of light in glass is 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, calculate the speed of light in (i) vacuum, (ii) water.
items.answer:

(i) n_glass = c / v_glass, so c = n_glass × v_glass = (4/3) × 2 × 10⁸ = 2.67 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
(ii) n_water = c / v_water, so v_water = c / n_water = (2.67 × 10⁸) ÷ (3/2) = (2 × 2.67 × 10⁸)/3 = 1.78 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: What is the difference between virtual images produced by concave, plane and convex mirror?
items.answer: The virtual image produced by a concave mirror is magnified, the virtual image produced by a plane mirror is of the same size as the object, and the virtual image produced by a convex mirror is diminished. In all three cases the image is erect and cannot be taken on a screen.

items.stem: A concave mirror is known as a converging mirror while a convex mirror is known as diverging mirror. Explain why?
items.answer: A concave mirror converges a parallel beam of light falling on it to a point (its focus), so it is known as a converging mirror. On the other hand, a convex mirror diverges a parallel beam falling on it (the reflected rays appear to come from its focus behind the mirror), so it is known as a diverging mirror.

items.stem: A light ray enters from medium A to medium B as shown in the figure. (a) Which one of the two media is denser w.r.t. the other medium? Justify your answer. (b) If the speed of light in medium A is v_A and in medium B is v_B, what is the refractive index of B with respect to A?

items.stem: The refractive index of a medium x with respect to medium y is 2/3 and the refractive index of medium y with respect to medium z is 4/3. Find the refractive index of medium z with respect to medium x. If the speed of light in medium x is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, calculate the speed of light in medium y.

The refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is the ratio of the speed of light in medium 1 to the speed of light in medium 2.

Also n_xy = v_y / v_x = 2/3, and v_x = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, so v_y = (2/3) × 3 × 10⁸ = 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
Hence the speed of light in medium y is 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A concave mirror produces three times enlarged real image of an object placed at 12 cm in front of it. Calculate the radius of curvature of the mirror.
items.answer:
Given u = –12 cm and, for a real enlarged image, m = –3.
m = –v/u → –3 = –v/(–12) → v = –36 cm.
Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u = 1/(–36) + 1/(–12) = (–1 – 3)/36 = –4/36, so f = –9 cm.
Radius of curvature R = 2f = 2 × (–9) = –18 cm, i.e. the radius of curvature is 18 cm.

items.stem: Why does a ray of light passing through the centre of curvature of a concave mirror, after reflection, is reflected back along the same path?
items.answer: It is because such an incident ray falls on the mirror along the normal to the reflecting surface (the normal at any point of a spherical mirror passes through its centre of curvature). Hence the angle of incidence is zero and, according to the law of reflection, the angle of reflection is always equal to the angle of incidence, so the angle of reflection is also zero. Therefore the reflected ray travels back along the same path.

items.stem: How can you identify the three types of mirrors without touching?
items.answer: By looking into the mirror and going close to it, the mirrors can be identified. If the image is of the same size and erect, it is a plane mirror. If the image is of bigger size and erect, it is a concave mirror. If the image is of smaller size and erect, it is a convex mirror.

items.stem: The diagram given below shows an object O and its image I. Copy the diagram and draw suitable ray to locate the lens and its focus. Name the type of lens used in this case.

Next draw a ray from O parallel to the principal axis; after refraction it appears to come from the focus on the same side as the object, which fixes F. items.stem: Name the type of mirror used in the following situations and support your answer with a reason: (i) Mirror used for shaving. (ii) Mirror used by ENT doctors. (iii) Mirror used in the vehicles for viewing the traffic approaching from behind.
items.answer: (i) Concave mirror. (ii) Concave mirror. Reason: when an object is held between the pole and the principal focus of a concave mirror, the mirror forms a virtual, erect and magnified image of the object. (iii) Convex mirror. Reason: the image formed by a convex mirror is always virtual, erect and smaller than the object, so it covers a large area (wide field of view).

items.stem: Why does a pencil immersed in water appear bent and short? Explain with the help of a ray diagram.
items.answer: It is due to the refraction of light. Consider a pencil AB such that the portion CB of the pencil is immersed in water. Rays of light from the tip B of the pencil bend away from the normal as they go from water into air. The refracted rays appear to come from the point B′, which lies above B. Thus the immersed portion of the pencil appears as CB′, i.e. the pencil looks bent at the water surface, and the immersed part also appears shorter than its actual length.

items.stem: (a) State laws of refraction. (b) A ray of light is incident normally to the surface of a glass slab placed in air. Find the angle of incidence and angle of refraction in this case.
items.answer:
(a) The laws of refraction of light are: (i) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface of the two transparent media at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. (ii) The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant, for light of a given colour and for a given pair of media: sin i / sin r = constant. This is Snell's law of refraction, and the constant is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.
(b) For normal incidence the ray travels along the normal, so ∠i = 0° and ∠r = 0°.

items.stem: State two uses of concave mirrors.

Lens formula: 1/v – 1/u = 1/f → 1/18 – 1/(–12) = 1/f → 1/18 + 1/12 = (2 + 3)/36 = 5/36 = 1/f, so f = 36/5 = 7.2 cm.
The image is formed on the other side of the lens, so it is real. Since f = 7.2 cm and u = –12 cm, the object lies between f and 2f, so the image is magnified and is formed beyond 2f. Also m = v/u = 18/(–12) = –3/2; as |m| = 3/2 > 1, the image is indeed magnified (and inverted).

items.stem: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm is placed at a distance of 24 cm from the screen. How far from the lens should an object be placed so as to form a real image on the screen? Also find the nature and magnification of the image produced by the lens.
items.answer:
Given f = +20 cm and v = +24 cm (image on the screen).
Lens formula: 1/v – 1/u = 1/f → –1/u = 1/f – 1/v = 1/20 – 1/24 = (6 – 5)/120 = 1/120, so u = –120 cm.
The object should be placed 120 cm from the lens.
Magnification m = v/u = 24/(–120) = –0.2. The negative sign indicates that the image is real and inverted, and |m| = 0.2 < 1 shows it is diminished (one-fifth the size of the object).

items.stem: (a) A ray of light is incident at an angle of 45° at the interface of medium (1) and medium (2) as shown in the above diagram. Redraw this diagram in the answer book and complete it. If the angle of refraction is 30°, find the refractive index of medium (2) with respect to medium (1). (Given that sin 45° = 1/√2 and sin 30° = 1/2) (b) If second medium is water in place of medium (2), will the angle of refraction increase or decrease? Why? (Refractive index of water = 4/3)
items.answer:
(a) In the completed diagram the refracted ray inside medium (2) is drawn bent towards the normal, making 30° with it. Using Snell's law,
₁n₂ = sin i / sin r = sin 45° / sin 30° = (1/√2) ÷ (1/2) = 2/√2 = √2 = 1.414.
So the refractive index of medium (2) with respect to medium (1) is 1.414.
(b) The angle of refraction will increase, because medium (2) with n = 1.414 is denser than water with n = 4/3 ≈ 1.33. In the rarer medium the ray bends less towards the normal, so the angle of refraction becomes larger.

items.stem: (a) What is meant by 'power of a lens'? (b) State its unit and define it. (c) Which of the two lenses has a greater power (i) a convex lens of focal length 5 cm or (ii) a convex lens of focal length 50 cm? Justify your answer.
items.answer:
(a) The power of a lens is its degree of convergence or divergence, and is represented as the reciprocal of the focal length of the lens expressed in metres: P = 1/f (m).
(b) The unit of power of a lens is the dioptre (D). One dioptre is the power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre.
(c) The convex lens of focal length 5 cm has the greater power, because P ∝ 1/f — the shorter the focal length, the greater the power. (Its power is 100/5 = +20 D against 100/50 = +2 D.)

items.stem: A convex lens forms a real image four times magnified at a distance of 60 cm from the lens. Calculate the focal length and the power of the lens.
items.answer:
For a real, inverted image that is four times magnified, m = –4 and v = +60 cm.
m = v/u → –4 = 60/u → u = –15 cm.
Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v – 1/u = 1/60 + 1/15 = (1 + 4)/60 = 5/60 = 0.083 cm⁻¹, so f = 12 cm = 0.12 m.
Power P = 1/f (in metres) = 1/0.12 = +8.33 D.

items.stem: (i) Where should an object be placed in case of a convex lens to form an image of same size as the object? Show with the help of a ray diagram the position and nature of the image formed. (ii) With the help of ray diagram, illustrate the change in position, nature and size of the image formed if the convex lens in case (i) is replaced by concave lens of same focal length. (iii) State the condition under which a light ray passes undeviated through a lens.
items.answer:
(i) The object should be placed at 2F in front of the convex lens. The image is then formed at 2F on the other side of the lens and is real, inverted and of the same size as the object.
(ii) If the convex lens is replaced by a concave lens of the same focal length, the image is formed between the optical centre and the focus on the same side of the lens as the object; it is virtual, erect and diminished.
(iii) A light ray passes undeviated when it passes through the optical centre of the lens.

items.stem: Which lens can be used as a magnifying glass? For which position of object does a convex lens form; (a) a virtual and erect image? (b) a real and inverted image of same size as that of object? Draw labelled ray diagrams to show the formation of the required images in each of the above two cases.
items.answer:
A convex lens can be used as a magnifying glass.
(a) A virtual and erect image is formed when the object is placed between the optical centre and the principal focus F₁ of the convex lens; the image is then virtual, erect and magnified, and lies on the same side of the lens as the object.
(b) A real and inverted image of the same size as the object is formed when the object is placed at 2F₁; the image is then formed at 2F₂ on the other side of the lens.

items.stem: (a) A compound lens is made of two lenses in contact having powers +12.5 D and –2.5 D. Find the focal length and power of the combination. (b) The magnification produced by a mirror is +1. What does this mean?
items.answer:
(a) P = P₁ + P₂ = 12.5 + (–2.5) = 10 D. Focal length f = 1/P = 1/10 = 0.1 m (i.e. 10 cm). So the combination behaves as a convex lens of power +10 D and focal length 10 cm.
(b) The '+' sign means the image is virtual and erect; the value 1 means the image is of exactly the same size as the object. This is the case of a plane mirror.

items.stem: Name the type of lens used to obtain; (i) an erect, enlarged and virtual image of an object. (ii) an erect, diminished and virtual image of an object. Draw labelled ray diagrams to show the formation of image in each case. Which of these lenses could also form a magnified and real image of the object? State the position of the object for which this could happen.
items.answer:
(i) Convex lens — with the object placed between the optical centre and the focus, it gives an erect, enlarged, virtual image.
(ii) Concave lens — for an object anywhere in front of it, it gives an erect, diminished, virtual image.
The convex lens can also form a real, inverted and magnified image. Position of the object for this: between F and 2F.

items.stem: (a) Define power of a lens and write its S.I. unit. (b) A convex lens of power 4 D is placed at a distance of 40 cm from a wall. At what distance from the lens should a candle be placed so that its image is formed on the wall?
items.answer:
(a) The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length expressed in metres. The S.I. unit of power is the dioptre (D).
(b) f = 1/P = 1/4 m = 25 cm, and v = +40 cm (the image falls on the wall).
Lens formula: 1/v – 1/u = 1/f → 1/u = 1/v – 1/f = 1/40 – 1/25 = (5 – 8)/200 = –3/200, so u = –200/3 cm ≈ –66.7 cm.
So the candle should be placed 200/3 cm (about 66.7 cm) from the lens.

items.stem: An object is placed at a distance 100 cm from a lens of power –4 D. Find the position and nature of image so formed.
items.answer:
Power of lens, P = –4 D, so focal length f = 100/(–4) = –25 cm. Object distance u = –100 cm.
Lens formula: 1/v – 1/u = 1/f → 1/v = 1/u + 1/f = 1/(–100) + 1/(–25) = (–1 – 4)/100 = –5/100, so v = –20 cm.
Magnification m = v/u = (–20)/(–100) = 1/5 = 0.2.
The image is formed 20 cm from the lens on the same side as the object; its nature is virtual, erect and diminished (one-fifth the size of the object).

items.stem: It is required to get (i) a magnified, erect and virtual image, (ii) a diminished, virtual and erect image of a given object. What type of lens should we use in each case and where should the object be kept? Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation in each case. Which of these lenses could also form a magnified, real and inverted image of an object? Also indicate the position of object for which this could happen.
items.answer:
(i) We need a convex lens for a magnified, erect and virtual image, and the object must be placed between the optical centre O and the focus F′.
(ii) We need a concave lens for a diminished, erect and virtual image, and the object may be placed anywhere in front of the lens.
A convex lens can also form a magnified, real and inverted image; this happens when the object is kept between F and 2F.

items.stem: (a) Name the kind of lens that can form; (i) an inverted magnified image, (ii) an erect diminished image. Draw ray diagrams to illustrate your answer in each case. (b) Draw a ray diagram to show the image formed of an object placed between f and 2f distances from a convex lens.
items.answer:
(a) (i) A convex lens forms an inverted magnified image, when the object is placed between F and 2F. (ii) A concave lens forms an erect diminished image, for an object placed anywhere in front of it.
(b) For an object placed between f and 2f of a convex lens, the ray diagram shows the image formed beyond 2f on the other side of the lens; it is real, inverted and magnified.

items.stem: (a) Define optical centre of a spherical lens. (b) You are given a convex lens of focal length 30 cm. Where would you place an object to get a real, inverted and highly enlarged image of the object? Draw a ray diagram showing the image formation. (c) A concave lens has a focal length of 20 cm. At what distance should an object be placed so that it forms an image at 15 cm away from the lens?
items.answer:
(a) The optical centre is the central point of the lens through which a ray of light passes without suffering any deviation.
(b) The object is placed at the focus F, i.e. at 30 cm from the lens. The refracted rays then emerge almost parallel, so the image is formed at infinity and is real, inverted and highly enlarged.
(c) Given f = –20 cm, v = –15 cm, u = ?
Using 1/f = 1/v – 1/u: 1/u = 1/v – 1/f = 1/(–15) + 1/20 = (–4 + 3)/60 = –1/60, so u = –60 cm.
The object should be placed 60 cm from the lens.

items.stem: One half of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm is covered with black paper. (i) Will the lens produce a complete image of the object? (ii) Show the formation of the image of an object placed at 2F₁ of such covered lens with the help of a ray diagram. (iii) What will happen to the intensity of the image formed by a convex lens which is partly covered with black paper?
items.answer:
(i) Yes, the lens will still produce a complete image of the object, because refraction still takes place through the uncovered half of the lens.
(ii) With the object at 2F₁, the ray diagram shows the image formed at 2F₂ on the other side; it is real, inverted and of the same size as the object.
(iii) The intensity (brightness) of the image decreases, because a smaller amount of light now passes through the lens.

items.stem: (a) An object is placed at the focus of a convex lens. Draw a ray diagram to locate the position of the image formed, if any, state its position and nature. (b) An object placed 50 cm from a lens produces a virtual image at a distance of 10 cm from the lens. Find the focal length of the lens and also state the type of the lens used.
items.answer:
(a) With the object at the focus of a convex lens the refracted rays emerge parallel to one another, so the image is formed at infinity. Position: at infinity. Nature: real and inverted (highly enlarged).
(b) Given v = –10 cm (virtual image, on the same side as the object) and u = –50 cm.
Lens formula: 1/v – 1/u = 1/f → –1/10 + 1/50 = (–5 + 1)/50 = –4/50 = 1/f, so f = –50/4 = –12.5 cm.
The focal length is negative, so the lens used is a concave (diverging) lens.

items.stem: (a) A divergent lens has focal length of 20 cm. At what distance should the object from the lens be placed so that an image is formed 10 cm away from the lens? What is the magnification produced by the lens? (b) Draw a ray diagram to show the position and nature of the image formed by a convex lens when an object is placed between optical centre and focus of the lens.
items.answer:
(a) For a divergent (concave) lens f = –20 cm, and its image is always virtual, so v = –10 cm.
Using 1/f = 1/v – 1/u: 1/u = 1/v – 1/f = –1/10 + 1/20 = (–2 + 1)/20 = –1/20, so u = –20 cm. The object should be placed 20 cm from the lens.
Magnification m = v/u = (–10)/(–20) = +0.5, i.e. the image is virtual, erect and half the size of the object.
(b) When the object lies between the optical centre and the focus of a convex lens, the ray diagram shows a virtual, erect and magnified image formed on the same side of the lens as the object.

items.stem: (a) Explain in brief, convex lens is converging in nature. (b) A convex lens forms a real and inverted image of a needle at a distance of 50 cm from it. Where is the needle placed in front of convex lens if the image is equal to the size of the object? Also find the power of the lens.
items.answer:
(a) A convex lens may be regarded as made up of a number of prisms together with a glass slab. The rays of light, after refraction through each prism, bend towards its base, so all the rays are brought together and converge at a point on the principal axis. Hence a convex lens is converging in nature.
(b) Given v = +50 cm. Since the image formed by the lens is real, inverted and of the same size as the object, the object must be at 2F and the image also at 2F.
So 2f = 50 cm → f = 25 cm, i.e. the needle is placed 50 cm in front of the lens.
Power P = 100/f (in cm) = 100/25 = +4 D.

items.stem:
(a) Define 1 dioptre of power. Find the focal length of a lens of power –2.0 D. (b) Why does a lemon kept in water in a glass tumbler appear to be bigger than its actual size? (c) Study the table given below and state the medium in which light ray will travel fastest. Why?
MediumABC
Refractive index1.331.52.4
items.answer:
(a) (i) One dioptre is the power of a lens of focal length one metre. (ii) Using P = 1/f: –2.0 D = 1/f (in m), so f = –0.5 m = –50 cm.
(b) This is due to the phenomenon of refraction of light. A ray of light starting from the lemon kept in water reaches the water–air interface and bends away from the normal. To the observer it appears as if the light ray is coming from a point above the actual point, and this apparent position makes the lemon appear bigger than its actual size.
(c) The light ray will travel fastest in medium A, because it is the medium with the least refractive index (1.33). Since v = c/n, the smaller the refractive index the greater the speed of light in the medium.

items.stem: (a) Draw a ray diagram to show the formation of image by a convex lens when an object is placed in front of the lens between its optical centre and principal focus. (b) In the above ray diagram mark the object-distance (u) and the image-distance (v) with their proper sign (+ve or –ve as per the new cartesian sign convention) and state how these distances are related to the focal length (f) of the convex lens in this case. (c) Find the power of a convex lens which forms a real and inverted image of magnification –1 of an object placed at a distance of 20 cm from optical centre.
items.answer:
(a) For an object placed between the optical centre and the principal focus of a convex lens, the ray diagram shows a virtual, erect and magnified image on the same side of the lens as the object.
(b) Here both u and v are negative while f is positive. They are related by the lens formula –1/u + 1/v = 1/f, i.e. 1/v – 1/u = 1/f.
(c) Magnification m = –1 and u = –20 cm. m = v/u → –1 = v/(–20) → v = +20 cm.
From the lens formula, 1/f = 1/v – 1/u = 1/20 – 1/(–20) = 2/20, so f = 10 cm = 0.1 m.
Power P = 1/f (in m) = 1/0.1 = +10 D.

items.stem: An object 4 cm in height is placed at 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed to obtain a sharp image of the object? Calculate the height of the image.
items.answer:
Given u = –15 cm, f = –10 cm, h_o = 4 cm.
Using the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u: 1/v = 1/f – 1/u = –1/10 + 1/15 = (–3 + 2)/30 = –1/30, so v = –30 cm.
The screen should be placed 30 cm in front of the mirror.
Magnification m = –v/u = –(–30)/(–15) = –2, and m = h_i/h_o, so h_i = –2 × 4 = –8 cm.
The image height will be 8 cm (the negative sign shows the image is real and inverted).

items.stem: A 3 cm tall object is placed 18 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed to see a sharp image of the object on the screen? Also calculate the height of the image formed.
items.answer:
Given u = –18 cm, f = –12 cm, h_o = 3 cm.
As we know, 1/f = 1/v + 1/u → 1/v = –1/12 + 1/18 = (–3 + 2)/36 = –1/36, so v = –36 cm.
The screen should be placed 36 cm in front of the mirror.
Magnification m = –v/u = –(–36)/(–18) = –2, and m = h_i/h_o, so h_i = –2 × 3 = –6 cm.
The image height will be 6 cm, and the image is real and inverted.

items.stem: The image of a candle flame placed at a distance of 30 cm from a mirror is formed on a screen placed in front of the mirror at a distance of 60 cm from its pole. What is the nature of the mirror? Find its focal length, if the height of the flame is 2.4 cm, find the height of its image. State whether the image formed is erect or inverted.
items.answer:
The image is caught on a screen, so it is real; hence the nature of the mirror is concave.
Given u = –30 cm, v = –60 cm, h_o = 2.4 cm.
Using the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u = –1/60 – 1/30 = –(1 + 2)/60 = –3/60, so f = –20 cm, i.e. the focal length is 20 cm.
Magnification m = –v/u = –(–60)/(–30) = –2, so h_i = m × h_o = –2 × 2.4 = –4.8 cm.
The required height of the image is 4.8 cm and, the value being negative, the image formed by the mirror is inverted.

items.stem: If the image formed by a lens for all positions of an object placed in front of it is always erect and diminished, what is the nature of the lens? Draw a diagram to justify your answer. If the numerical value of the power of this lens is 10 D, what is its focal length in the cartesian system?
items.answer:
If the image formed by a lens for all positions of the object in front of it is always virtual, erect and diminished, the lens is a concave (diverging) lens. The ray diagram shows the diverged rays appearing to come from a point between the optical centre and the focus on the object's side.
For a concave lens the power is negative, so P = –10 D.
P = 1/f (in metres) → –10 = 1/f → f = –0.1 m = –10 cm.
In the cartesian system the focal length is –10 cm.

items.stem: Draw ray diagram to show the formation of three times magnified (i) real and (ii) virtual image of an object by a converging lens. Mark the position of O, F and 2F in each diagram.
items.answer:
(i) Real image three times magnified: the object is placed between F and 2F (at a distance 4f/3 from the lens). The ray parallel to the principal axis is refracted through F, and the ray through O goes straight; they meet beyond 2F on the other side, giving a real, inverted image three times the size of the object.
(ii) Virtual image three times magnified: the object is placed between O and F (at a distance 2f/3 from the lens). The refracted rays diverge and, produced backwards, meet on the same side as the object, giving a virtual, erect image three times the size of the object.
In both diagrams the optical centre O and the points F and 2F are marked on either side of the lens.

items.stem: (i) Define optical centre of a spherical lens. (ii) A divergent lens has a focal length of 20 cm. At what distance should an object of height 4 cm from the optical centre of the lens be placed so that its image is formed 10 cm away from the lens? Find the size of the image also. (iii) Draw a ray diagram to show the formation of image in above situation.
items.answer:
(i) Optical centre: it is the central point of the lens through which a ray of light passes without suffering any deviation.
(ii) Given f = –20 cm, h_o = 4 cm, v = –10 cm (the image of a divergent lens is virtual).
Using 1/f = 1/v – 1/u: 1/u = 1/v – 1/f = –1/10 + 1/20 = (–2 + 1)/20 = –1/20, so u = –20 cm. The object should be placed 20 cm from the optical centre.
Size of image h_i = (v/u) × h_o = (–10/–20) × 4 = 2 cm, so the image is 2 cm tall, virtual and erect.
(iii) The ray diagram shows the diminished, erect, virtual image formed between the optical centre and the focus on the same side of the lens as the object.

items.stem: "A lens can form a magnified erect image as well as magnified inverted image of an object placed in front of it." State the nature of this lens and draw ray diagrams to justify the above statement. Mark the positions of O, F and 2F in the diagram.
items.answer:
The lens is a convex (converging) lens — a convex lens is used to form a magnified erect image as well as a magnified inverted image of an object.
Magnified and erect image: when the object is placed between the optical centre O and the focus F (within the focal length), the image formed is virtual, erect and magnified, on the same side of the lens as the object.
Magnified and inverted image: when the object is placed between F and 2F, the image formed is real, inverted and magnified, beyond 2F on the other side of the lens.
In both ray diagrams the positions of O, F and 2F are marked on the principal axis.

items.stem: The image formed by a spherical mirror is real, inverted and is of magnification −2. If the image is at a distance of 30 cm from the mirror, where is the object placed? Find the focal length of the mirror. List two characteristics of the image formed if the object is moved 10 cm towards the mirror.
items.answer:
Given, m = −2, v = −30 cm, u = ?
m = −v/u
−2 = −(−30)/u
u = −30/2 = −15 cm
The object is at 15 cm in front of the mirror.
By using the mirror formula,
1/v + 1/u = 1/f
−1/30 − 1/15 = 1/f
(−1 − 2)/30 = −3/30 = −1/10 = 1/f
f = −10 cm
The focal length is 10 cm (concave mirror).
If the object is moved 10 cm towards the mirror it lies 5 cm from the pole, i.e. within the focus, so the image will be (i) virtual and erect and (ii) enlarged in size.

items.stem: A mirror is fitted in a wall of the AGRA FORT. When you stand at a proper location, a full-size image of the Taj Mahal can be seen in this mirror. (a) What kind of mirror is it? (b) Draw a ray diagram for such a mirror when the object is at infinity.
items.answer:
(a) The mirror is a convex mirror.
(b) For a convex mirror with the object at infinity, the rays coming parallel to the principal axis appear to diverge from the principal focus F behind the mirror. The image is formed at the focus behind the mirror and is virtual, erect and highly diminished (point-sized).

items.stem: You are given a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Where will you place an object to get a real, inverted and highly enlarged image of the object? Draw a ray diagram.
items.answer: We know that a real, inverted and highly enlarged image of an object is formed by a convex lens if the object is placed at the focus of the lens. That is, the distance of the object from the optical centre of the lens is equal to the focal length of the lens = 10 cm. items.stem: Explain with the help of diagram why a pencil partly immersed in water appears to be bent at the water surface.
items.answer: It is due to the refraction of light. Consider a pencil AB such that the portion CB of the pencil is immersed in water. Rays of light from the tip B of the pencil bend away from the normal as they go from water into air. The refracted rays appear to come from the point B′. Thus the immersed portion of the pencil in water appears as CB′, and hence the pencil appears to be bent at the water surface. Moreover, the immersed portion of the pencil also appears to be shorter than the actual length of the pencil.

items.stem: (a) Draw a labelled ray diagram to show the path of a ray of light incident obliquely on one face of a glass slab. (b) Calculate the refractive index of the material of a glass. Given that the speed of light through the glass slab is 2 × 10⁸ m/s and in air is 3 × 10⁸ m/s. (c) Calculate the focal length of a lens, if its power is −2.5 D.
items.answer:
(a) The ray diagram shows the incident ray striking the first face obliquely, bending towards the normal inside the slab, emerging from the opposite face parallel to the incident ray and laterally displaced from it.
(b) Speed of light in glass slab, v = 2 × 10⁸ m/s; speed of light in air, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
n = c/v = (3 × 10⁸)/(2 × 10⁸) = 1.5
Hence, refractive index of material of glass slab is 1.5.
(c) Power, P = −2.5 D; focal length, f = ?
P = 1/f
f = 1/P = 1/(−2.5) = 100 cm/(−2.5) = −40 cm = −0.4 m
The focal length of a lens of power −2.5 D is −0.4 m or −40 cm.

The ray parallel to the principal axis is refracted through F and the ray through the optical centre goes straight; the refracted rays diverge and, produced backwards, meet on the same side of the lens as the object.

items.stem: A person suffering from myopia (near-sightedness) was advised to wear corrective lens of power –2.5 D. A spherical lens of same focal length was taken in the laboratory. At what distance should a student place an object from this lens so that it forms an image at a distance of 10 cm from the lens?
items.answer:
Given P = –2.5 D.
P = 1/f → f = 1/P = 1/(–2.5) = –0.4 m = –40 cm.
The lens is concave, so the image is virtual: v = –10 cm, u = ?
Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v – 1/u → 1/u = 1/v – 1/f = 1/(–10) – 1/(–40) = –1/10 + 1/40 = (–4 + 1)/40 = –3/40, so u = –40/3 = –13.33 cm.
The object should be placed 13.33 cm from the lens so that it forms an image at a distance of 10 cm from the lens.

items.stem: Prove that for a concave mirror the radius of curvature is twice its focal length.
items.answer:
Let NM be a ray made incident on the mirror parallel to the principal axis; after reflection it passes through the focus F. CM is the normal at M (the normal passes through the centre of curvature C).
∠1 = ∠2 (laws of reflection) …(1)
∠1 = ∠3 (alternate interior angles, NM being parallel to the axis CP) …(2)
From (1) and (2), ∠3 = ∠2.
Therefore ΔCFM is an isosceles triangle, so CF = FM …(3)
For a mirror of small aperture, M lies very close to the pole P, so FM = PF …(4)
From (3) and (4), CF = PF.
Now CP = CF + PF = PF + PF = 2PF, i.e. R = 2f.
Hence for a concave mirror the radius of curvature is twice its focal length.

items.stem: An object is kept in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. The image is three times the size of the object. Calculate two possible distances of the object from the mirror.
items.answer:
Given, f = −20 cm.
For a real image, m = −3:
−3 = −v/u  ⇒  v = 3u
1/v + 1/u = 1/f
1/(3u) + 1/u = 1/(−20)
4/(3u) = −1/20
3u = −80  ⇒  u = −80/3 = −26.6 cm
For a virtual image, m = +3:
+3 = −v/u  ⇒  v = −3u
1/v + 1/u = 1/f
1/(−3u) + 1/u = 1/(−20)
2/(3u) = 1/(−20)
u = −40/3 = −13.33 cm
So the two possible object distances are 26.6 cm and 13.33 cm from the mirror.

1/f = 1/v + 1/u
1/v = 1/f − 1/u
Putting the values of u and f,

items.stem: (a) State the laws of refraction. (b) What is meant by the term absolute refractive index? The speed of light in a transparent medium is 0.6 times that of the speed in vacuum. Find refractive index of the medium. (c) How should a ray of light be incident on a rectangular glass slab so that it comes out from the opposite side of the slab without being displaced? Draw a ray diagram to illustrate your answer.
items.answer:
(a) The following are the laws of refraction of light:
(i) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface of two transparent media at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane.
(ii) The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant, for the light of a given colour and for the given pair of media. This law is also known as Snell's law of refraction. If i is the angle of incidence and r is the angle of refraction, then sin i / sin r = constant. This constant value is called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.
(b) (i) The absolute refractive index of a medium is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in the medium.
(ii) The speed of light in vacuum = c; the speed of light in the medium = 0.6c
n = (speed of light in vacuum)/(speed of light in the medium) = c/(0.6c) = 1.66
(c) The ray of light should be incident normally (perpendicularly, at an angle of incidence of 0°) to the surface of the glass slab. It then passes straight through the slab without bending and emerges from the opposite side along the same line, with no lateral displacement.

(b) Given, u = −16 cm, f = +12 cm, h_o = 2 cm.

Formula, 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 − 1/15 = (3 − 2)/30 = 1/30
So v = 30 cm
Magnification, m = h′/h = v/u
h′/2.0 = 30/(−15) = −2
h′ = −4.0 cm
The nature of the image is real, inverted and enlarged; it is formed at a distance of 30 cm on the right side (the other side) of the lens and is 4.0 cm in size.

items.stem: A needle placed 45 cm from a lens forms an image on a screen placed 90 cm on the other side of the lens. Identify the type of lens. Determine its focal length and the power. What is the size of image, if needle is 5 cm in height?
items.answer:
Since the image formed is on the other side of the lens and can be caught on a screen (real image), the lens is a convex lens.
Here, u = −45 cm and v = 90 cm.
1/f = 1/v − 1/u = (1/90) − (−1/45) = (1 + 2)/90 = 3/90 = 1/30
f = 30 cm = 0.30 m
Power, P = 1/f (in metres) = 1/0.30 = +3.33 D
m = v/u = 90/(−45) = −2
m = h_i/h_o  ⇒  −2 = h_i/5  ⇒  h_i = −10 cm
So the image is real, inverted and 10 cm in height.

items.stem: (i) To construct a ray diagram we use two rays which are so chosen that it is easy to know their directions after reflection from the mirror. List two such rays and state the path of these rays after reflection in case of concave mirrors. Use these two rays and draw ray diagrams to locate the image of an object placed between pole and focus of a concave mirror. (ii) A concave mirror produces three times magnified image on a screen. If the object is placed 20 cm in front of the mirror, how far is the screen from the object.
items.answer:
(i) Two light rays whose paths after reflection are known are:
(a) The incident ray passing through the centre of curvature — after reflecting from the concave mirror the light moves back along the same path (because it strikes the mirror normally).
(b) The ray incident obliquely towards the pole of the mirror — the incident ray is reflected back by the reflecting surface of the concave mirror obliquely, making an equal angle with the principal axis.
Using these two rays, for an object placed between the focus and the pole of a concave mirror the reflected rays diverge and their backward extensions meet behind the mirror, so the image is virtual, erect and magnified.
(ii) The image is formed on a screen, so it is real and inverted: m = −3 and u = −20 cm.
m = −v/u  ⇒  −3 = −v/(−20)  ⇒  v = −60 cm
The screen is 60 cm from the mirror, so its distance from the object is 60 − 20 = 40 cm.
items.ocr: The printed material carries only part (i) — the two rays plus three ray diagrams (the third one appearing on page 50 through the column layout). No worked solution for part (ii) survives in the print/OCR, so the numerical answer (v = −60 cm, screen 40 cm from the object) was derived from the printed data.

items.stem: (i) If the image formed by a mirror for all positions of the object placed in front of it is always diminished, erect and virtual, state the type of the mirror and also draw a ray diagram to justify your answer. Write one use such mirrors are put to and why. (ii) Define the radius of curvature of spherical mirrors. Find the nature and focal length of a spherical mirror whose radius of curvature is +24 cm.
items.answer:
(i) A convex mirror forms an erect, diminished and virtual image for all the positions of the object placed in front of it. Convex mirrors are commonly used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles, as they always give an erect, though diminished, image and hence cover a much wider field of view of the traffic behind.
(ii) The radius of the sphere of which the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror forms a part is called the radius of curvature of the mirror.
Given R = +24 cm. Since the radius of curvature is positive, the mirror is a convex mirror.
f = R/2 = 24/2 = 12 cm
Thus, the focal length of the convex spherical mirror is 12 cm.

Also 'infront' expanded to 'in front'. The printed solution gives R = 24 cm and f = 24/2 = 12 cm and states the mirror is convex.

(iv) An object is placed at a distance of 18 cm from the pole of a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm. Find the position of the image formed in this case.

(i) Case 1. Here the object distance (45 cm) is greater than the radius of curvature of the mirror (R = 2f = 40 cm), i.e. the object is placed beyond the centre of curvature. Hence the image formed by the mirror is diminished, real and inverted.
(ii) For mirror B, R = 2f = 2 × 15 = 30 cm. Hence the object is placed at the centre of curvature of the mirror. The size of the image is the same as that of the object, and the image is real and inverted.
(iii) In case 3: u = −20 cm, f = −30 cm. By the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f → 1/v + 1/(−20) = 1/(−30), which gives v = 60 cm. The nature of the image is virtual and erect, and it is magnified.
(iv) Given u = −18 cm, f = −12 cm. From the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f → 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/(−12) − 1/(−18) = −1/36, so v = −36 cm. The image is formed 36 cm in front of the mirror (on the same side as the object).

(c) Name the type of mirror used by dentists. Give reason why do they use such type of mirrors. (d) Look at the table and identify the situation (object distance and focal length) which resembles the situation in which concave mirrors are used as shaving mirrors? Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation in this case.

(b) In Case II, since the object (30 cm) is placed at the centre of curvature (R = 2f = 2 × 15 = 30 cm), the image is real, inverted and of the same size as the object.

items.stem:
A concave mirror forms image of an object thrice in its size on a screen. Magnification of a mirror gives information about the size of the image relative to the object. It is defined as the ratio of size of image to the size of object. It is represented by m.

m = (Size of image) / (Size of object)

Sign of magnification by mirror gives the information about the nature of the image produced by it.
(i) Describe the nature of image formed.
(ii) If the object is x distance from the pole of mirror, then find image distance from the pole.
(iii) If the radius of curvature of mirror is R, then write the relation between object distance, image distance and focal length of the mirror.
(iv) Give one use of concave mirror.
items.answer:
(i) Since the image is formed on a screen, it must be real; as it is three times the size of the object it is real, inverted and magnified, so m = −3.
(ii) Here u = −x and m = −v/u, so −3 = −v/(−x), giving v = −3x. The image is at a distance 3x from the pole, in front of the mirror.
(iii) Using the mirror formula with f = R/2: 1/(3x) + 1/x = 2/R (as printed).
(iv) A concave mirror is used in search lights and in the headlights of automobiles.

items.stem:
A concave lens is thick at the edges and thin at the centre, while a convex lens is thick at the centre and thin at the edges. We can distinguish between a concave lens and a convex lens without touching them. For this keep a book close to a lens and observe the image of the text of the book through the lens. If the letters appear enlarged, then it is a convex lens and if the letters appear diminished then it is a concave lens. Convex lens converges light rays and hence known as converging lens. Similarly, concave lens diverges light rays and is known as diverging lens. Linear magnification produced by a lens is equal to the ratio of the image distance to the object distance. Power of a lens is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length.
(i) What type of image is always made by a concave lens?
(ii) If magnification produced by a spherical lens is +0.75, then what is the nature of the lens?
(iii) What is the power of a convex lens with focal length 80 cm?
(iv) What kind of lens is present in human eye?
items.answer:
(i) A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image of an object.
(ii) Here m = +0.75 (less than 1), so the image formed is smaller than the object, i.e. diminished, and the positive sign shows it is virtual and erect. A virtual, erect and diminished image can be formed only by a concave lens, so the lens is concave.
(iii) P = 1/f (in metres) = (1/80) × 100 = +1.25 D.
(iv) A converging (convex) lens is present in the human eye.
items.ocr: LaTeX display maths for the power calculation rewritten inline. The page-54 image next to this question is the publisher's QR-code advertisement ('NO NEED TO PURCHASE SAMPLE PAPERS ... SCAN QR CODE'), so it is page furniture and is not attached; that advertising text was stripped from the stem/answer.

items.stem:
When a light ray goes from one transparent medium to another transparent medium, it suffers a change in direction on entering the second medium. The phenomenon of change in the path of light rays when going from one medium to another medium is known as refraction. The extent of the bending for a given pair of media can be expressed in terms of refractive index. The refractive index is related to an important physical quantity, the relative speed of light in different media.

(i) When light goes from one medium to another, which of the three parameters - frequency, wavelength, velocity - change?
(ii) A ray of light enters into the glass from air. Does it bend towards normal?
(iii) Light enters from air to glass having refractive index 1.50. What is the speed of light in the glass? The speed of light in vacuum is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
(iv) What is the unit of refractive index?
items.answer:
(i) Two parameters change - wavelength and velocity. The frequency remains unchanged.
(ii) Yes, it bends towards the normal, because glass is optically denser than air.
(iii) Refractive index of a medium, nₘ = (speed of light in vacuum)/(speed of light in the medium) = c/v. Here c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and n_g = 1.50, so v = c/n_g = (3 × 10⁸)/1.50 = 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
(iv) Refractive index has no unit (it is a ratio of two speeds).

Ray is a given pair of media can be expressed in terms of refractive index') - the two sentences were untangled without adding new content. items.stem:
Convex mirror is used as a rear view mirror in vehicles. Since the image of the object formed is small in size, the field of view is increased. Convex mirror is also used in street lights to diverge light over a large area.

(i) In driver's mirror, what type of image is formed behind the vehicle?
(ii) What can you say about field of view of a convex mirror?
(iii) A convex mirror is used to form the image of an object. What is the nature of formed image?
items.answer:
(i) A convex mirror forms an erect and diminished (virtual) image of an object behind the vehicle.
(ii) The field of view of a convex mirror is large (wider than that of a plane or concave mirror of the same size).
(iii) The image formed by a convex mirror is virtual, erect and diminished.
items.ocr: The printed key for (iii) says 'The image is real', which contradicts its own passage and its answer (i) ('erect and diminished' image behind the vehicle) - a convex mirror always forms a virtual image, so the corrected answer 'virtual, erect and diminished' is given. Passage figure on page 53 attached.

items.stem:
Lenses are objects made of transparent materials such as glass or clear plastic that have curved surfaces. Diverging lenses are thicker at their edges than at their centres and make light rays passing through them spread out. Converging lenses are thicker in their middle than at their edges and make light rays passing through them focus at a point. These are used in spectacles to help people with poor vision see better. The converging lenses magnify by bending the rays of light that pass through them to meet at a point called focus. The thicker the converging lens is at its centre, the more it magnifies and the closer the focus is to the lens.

(i) Ravi uses two lenses A and B of same size and same material as shown. P₁ and P₂ are the powers of A and B. An object is kept at the same distance from the lens, between F and 2F of each lens on the principal axis in turn. Let I₁ and I₂ be the images formed by the two lenses respectively. What is the relation of image distances of both lenses?
(a) Distance of image I₂ will be less than distance of I₁ from the lens.
(b) Distance of image I₂ will be greater than distance of I₁ from the lens.
(c) Size of image I₁ will be equal to size of I₂.
(d) Size of image I₂ will be less than size of I₁.
(ii) Write down the relation between the power of lens of both lenses.
(iii) Meenakshi uses above two lenses A and B along with another two lenses C and D, as shown. She is able to see the subject matter on the black board while sitting in the front row in the classroom but is unable to see the same matter while sitting in the last row. Which of the above four lenses will she require to correct the defect in her vision? Why?
(iv) Natasha places an object on the principal axis of above given lens A. One end of this object coincides with the focus F and the other end with 2F. What will be the nature of the image formed by the lens on the other side?
items.answer:
(i) Option (a) - distance of image I₂ will be less than the distance of I₁ from the lens (B is the thicker lens, so it has the shorter focal length and forms its image nearer to the lens).
(ii) P₁ < P₂, because lens B is thicker at the centre, has a smaller focal length and therefore a greater power.
(iii) She will require lens C, because she is suffering from myopia (short-sightedness) and a concave (diverging) lens is required to correct myopia.
(iv) The image will be formed between 2F and infinity on the other side; the end at 2F images at 2F and the end at F images at infinity, so the image will be enlarged and stretched out - infinite in size (real and inverted).

items.stem:
The image formed by a convex lens depends on the position of the object in front of the lens. When the object is placed anywhere between focus and infinity, the image formed by convex lens is real and inverted. The image is not obtained on the screen when the object is placed between the focus and the lens. The distance between the optical centre O of the convex lens and the focus point F₁ and F₂ is its focal length. When the object shifts from −∞ to F₁, the image moves from F₂ to +∞. When the object shifts from F₁ to O, the image moves from −∞ to O. A student did an experiment with a convex lens. He put an object at different distances from the lens. In each case, he measured the distance of the image from the lens. The results were recorded in the following table.
Object distance (in cm)Image distance (in cm)
25100

Unfortunately, his results are written in the wrong order. (i) What is the focal length of this lens? (ii) Rewrite the image distances in the correct order. (iii) What is the minimum distance between an object and its real image formed by a convex lens?
items.answer:
(i) When the object distance equals the image distance, the object and image are both at twice the focal length from the lens. In the table this pair is 60 cm, so 2f = 60 cm would give f = 30 cm; but an object placed at the focus (30 cm) would give an image at infinity, and no such observation appears in the table, so f = 30 cm is not possible. Taking 2f = 40 cm gives f = 20 cm, which is the focal length of the lens.
(ii) Correct order of image distances: 100, 60, 40, 30, 24.
(iii) The minimum distance between an object and its real image formed by a convex lens is 4f.

items.stem:
Is there a relationship between the radius of curvature R, and focal length f, of a spherical mirror? For spherical mirrors of small apertures, the radius of curvature is found to be equal to twice the focal length. We put this as R = 2f. This implies that the principal focus of a spherical mirror lies midway between the pole and centre of curvature.
(i) Write relation between radius of curvature and focal length.
(ii) For which type of mirrors above relation is verified?
(iii) What should be size of the aperture?
(iv) Where does the principal focus of a spherical mirror lie?
items.answer:
(i) R = 2f (the radius of curvature is twice the focal length).
(ii) Spherical mirrors (both concave and convex).
(iii) The aperture should be small.
(iv) Midway between the pole and the centre of curvature of the mirror.

items.stem:
"Change in path of a light ray as it passes from one medium to another medium is called refraction of light." When light travels from a rarer medium to a denser one, it bends towards the normal (i > r) and when it travels from a denser medium to a rarer one, it bends away from the normal (i < r), where i = angle of incidence and r = angle of refraction. We can see refraction in our daily life; some of the examples are given below. The bottom of a tank or pond containing water appears to be raised due to refraction of light which takes place when light rays pass from the pool of water into the air. The letters appear to be raised when viewed through a glass slab placed over the document because of refraction of light. When a light ray enters a glass slab, then the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but it is shifted sideways slightly. In this case, refraction takes place twice: first when the ray enters the glass slab from air and second when it exits from the glass slab to air.
(i) What do you mean by optically rarer and denser medium?
(ii) What is the cause of refraction?
(iii) Draw a ray diagram showing refraction through a glass slab.
(iv) Give one example of refraction from our daily life experience other than the two examples given above.
items.answer:
(i) A medium in which the speed of light is more is known as an optically rarer medium, and a medium in which the speed of light is lesser is known as an optically denser medium.
(ii) The speed of light is different in different media - it is lesser in a denser medium and higher in a rarer medium. So when light enters a denser medium its speed reduces and it bends towards the normal, and when it enters a rarer medium its speed increases and it bends away from the normal.
(iii) Ray diagram of a glass slab: the incident ray strikes face AB making angle of incidence i, bends towards the normal inside the slab (angle of refraction r), and on leaving the opposite face it bends away from the normal, emerging with angle of emergence e = i, parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced.
(iv) A lemon kept in water in a glass tumbler appears to be bigger than its actual size when viewed from the sides.
items.ocr: LaTeX inline maths ($i > r$, $i < r$) rewritten as plain text; the stray 'h' artefacts after '$( i < r )$' and 'image distance ^ v h' style OCR noise removed. items.stem:
While dealing with the reflection of light by spherical mirrors, we shall follow a set of sign conventions called the New Cartesian Sign Convention. In this convention, the pole (P) of the mirror is taken as the origin. The principal axis of the mirror is taken as the x-axis of the coordinate system. In a spherical mirror, the distance of the object from its pole is called the object distance (u). The distance of the image from the pole of the mirror is called the image distance (v). Magnification produced by a spherical mirror gives the relative extent to which the image of an object is magnified with respect to the object size. It is expressed as the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object. It is usually represented by the letter m. (In the sign-convention diagram: distances measured along the direction of the incident light are positive and those measured against the direction of the incident light are negative; heights measured upwards, perpendicular to the principal axis, are positive and those measured downwards are negative.)
(i) How can you calculate the magnification of a spherical mirror?
(ii) What does a negative sign in the value of magnification indicate?
(iii) Find the focal length of a convex mirror whose radius of curvature is 32 cm.
(iv) Why is the height of the object taken to be positive?
items.answer:
(i) If h is the height of the object and h′ is the height of the image, then the magnification m produced by a spherical mirror is m = (height of the image h′)/(height of the object h), i.e. m = h′/h.
(ii) A negative sign in the value of the magnification indicates that the image is real (and inverted).
(iii) Radius of curvature of the convex mirror R = 32 cm, and R = 2 × focal length (f), so f = 32/2 = 16 cm. The focal length of the convex mirror is 16 cm.
(iv) As the object is usually placed above the principal axis, the height of the object is measured upwards and is therefore taken to be positive.

Harish is a student of class X. He is very passionate about doing science experiments. Recently, he visited Delhi with his parents to witness a science fair. He purchased different types of lenses, mirrors and other articles. One day, during games period, a student of the same class fell down and his lips started bleeding. On observation, it was found by the Physical Education teacher that very fine pieces of glass, difficult to observe, were stranded over there. Harish immediately rushed to the Physics Lab and brought a lens. The bigger image of the stranded glass pieces eased the first aid job.
(i) Name the lens and mirror bought by Harish.
(ii) Draw the ray diagram showing formation of very big image of object by lens. What should be the position of object to get such image?
items.answer:
(i) Harish brought a double convex (converging) lens, because it forms a magnified image and thus helps to see the fine pieces of glass; the corresponding mirror that magnifies in the same way is a concave mirror.
(ii) To get a very big (highly enlarged), virtual and erect image with a convex lens, the object must be placed between the optical centre O and the focus F₁ of the lens (i.e. within the focal length). The ray diagram shows the refracted rays diverging after the lens and meeting, when produced backwards, to form an enlarged virtual image on the same side as the object.

items.stem:
In a small town fair Amit took his friend and showed him a mirror in which his image showed upper half body very fat and lower body very thin. Amit's friend got upset but Amit explained him by showing his similar image in the mirror.
(i) Name two mirrors used in this fair shop.
(ii) Name the mirror in which the size of image is small.

(i) What is the focal length of the convex lens? Give reason in support of your answer. (ii) Write the serial number of that observation which is not correct. How did you arrive at this conclusion? (iii) Take an appropriate scale to draw ray diagram for the observation at S. No. 4 and find the approximate value of magnification.
items.answer:
(i) From S. No. 3 we can say that the radius of curvature of the lens is 30 cm, because when an object is placed at the centre of curvature of a convex lens its image is formed on the other side of the lens at the same distance from the lens. As the focal length is half of the radius of curvature, the focal length of the lens is +15 cm.
(ii) S. No. 6 is not correct. Here the object distance (10 cm) lies between the focus and the optical centre, so the image formed must be virtual; but in this observation a real image is shown, since the image distance is positive.
(iii) For object distance u = −20 cm and image distance v = +60 cm, the approximate value of magnification is 3 (the image is real, inverted and three times the size of the object), i.e. m = −3 in magnitude 3.
